newsitem.title: USA: Danny punches across tip of Louisiana, heads east.
newsitem.headline: Danny punches across tip of Louisiana, heads east.

text.p: Hurricane Danny punched across the tip of Louisiana early on Friday, flooding highways and flattening power lines with winds gusting up to 100 miles an hour, authorities said.

No deaths or serious injuries have been reported in Louisiana, but the National Hurricane Centre in Miami said the hurricane could spawn tornadoes as it swept across the Mississippi Delta and moved back into the Gulf of Mexico.

Lower Plaquemines Parish, southeast of New Orleans, took the brunt of the storm early Friday as the eye of the slow-moving hurricane drifted back into the Gulf of Mexico, dumping up to 10 inches of rain on the area as it moved northeast.
In New Orleans, the impact was limited to occasional showers and wind gusts as the city was spared the heavy rains that could have caused widespread flooding.
Plaquemines officials closed the only highway running the length of the parish Friday morning as high water made driving conditions extremely dangerous, a sheriff's deputy told Reuters.
"We don't have any injuries reported, and so far, thank God, no major property damage, but I really don't have time to talk," he said, not having time to give his name.
No evacuations were ordered for the parish.

West of Plaquemines, officials in Grand Isle, the state's only inhabited barrier island, reported heavy damage and erosion. Most of the island's 1,530 residents obeyed a mandatory evacuation order Thursday and moved inland to wait out the storm.
Grand Isle Mayor Pro Tem Ray Santini told Reuters the island is severely flooded and officials do not know when residents will be allowed to return.

Hurricane warning flags were raised from Morgan City, La., east to Destin, Fla., as the storm swept across the southern tip of Louisiana and moved back into the Gulf of Mexico's Breton Sound wildlife area.

The storm first made landfall overnight between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River, and the eye of the hurricane at 7 a.m. CDT was located about 45 miles southeast of New Orleans near latitude 29.6 north, longitude 89.5 west.

As it drifts northeast at about five miles an hour, the storm was on a track to again make landfall along the Gulf Coast between Mississippi and the Florida Panhandle, the National Hurricane Centre said.

Hurricane force winds of 75 miles an hour extended outward about 25 miles from the centre and tropical storm force winds extended up to 115 miles from the centre, with the strongest gusts on the east side of the slow-moving storm.
Danny could dump between 10 and 20 inches of rain in coastal areas of southeast Louisiana, where a storm surge four to five feet above normal tides threatened low-lying areas.

Evacuations were ordered in parts of Terrebonne and Lafourche parishes southwest of New Orleans, but people in some areas began returning to their homes Thursday night as the storm moved off to the east.
In low-lying St. Bernard Parish, southeast of New Orleans, officials handed out sandbags to seal off flood-prone roads and recommended that residents move to higher ground.

"If we get an east or northeast wind, it could really push some water into parts of the parish outside of the hurricane protection levees," Mike Sanders, spokesman for the St. Bernard Parish sheriff's department, said.

In New Orleans, late-night revellers on Bourbon Street barely broke stride as light rains and intermittent gusts swept the historic French Quarter. Even though officials had feared flooding in the city, which is below sea level, Danny hit the Big Easy with a weak punch.
